Redesigned Safely

Where a B2B Website Redesign Loses Traffic

The ProblemStandard Agency

Old URLs stop resolving and rankings die

The page structure changes and the old addresses stop resolving. Pages that took years to earn their rankings return errors, and the traffic they carried does not find its way back on its own.

Structured data treated as a launch-week detail

Structured data and search snippets get treated as a launch-week detail. On day one an engine loses the machine-readable version of a site it already understood.

Nothing was measured before the rebuild

The old site was only ever judged on taste, so the new one gets judged the same way. Six months later nobody can say what the redesign earned.

The SolutionThe Legency Approach

Earned traffic arrives at the new site on day one

A crawl of the live site produces the full 301 map before launch, so each old address arrives at the page that replaces it and the rankings travel with it.

Engines still understand the site at launch

Structured data and search snippets are rebuilt on the new templates before launch, and the pages that never had them get them for the first time, so nothing is lost on day one.

The result goes to the board as arithmetic

Rankings, conversion and a 100-point readability score are recorded on the old site and re-run identically on the new one, so what the redesign earned is a comparison rather than an opinion.

What Carries Over

Four Things You Keep Through the Redesign

The Rankings You Earned

Every live URL mapped to its new home before launch. On one six-site estate, 261 URLs stranded on a retired domain were mapped to the brands that should own them.

A Site Engines Can Still Read

Markup rebuilt on the new templates and re-checked after launch. Across that same estate, 230 markup errors were closed and technical health rose on all five sites measured in month one, by 5 to 10 points each.

Proof the Redesign Worked

A 100-point readability audit is run before the rebuild and re-run identically after it. One client moved from 30 to 59 in two months on that scale, our own audit both times.

No Rebuild in Two Years

The new site ships as a governed component library, so the round of change after this one is your marketing team adding pages instead of another rebuild.

Before You Commit

Most Redesigns Solve a Problem Nobody Diagnosed

A redesign is the most expensive answer available, and it is usually chosen before anyone has established what is actually wrong. These are the four reasons we hear, and what each one really needs.

"It looks dated"

Sometimes true and rarely the reason revenue is flat. Worth checking what the site does on mobile, how fast it is, and whether the copy still describes what you sell, before spending on a new look for the same problems.

"We have repositioned"

The strongest reason on this list. When what you sell has genuinely changed, the structure has to change with it, and patching the old structure produces a site that argues with itself.

"Nobody converts"

This is a conversion problem and a redesign is the slowest way to address it. It also destroys the attribution: change everything at once and you can never say which change did the work.

"Marketing cannot change anything"

A build problem rather than a design one. If the reason for the redesign is that the current site is unmaintainable, say so, because it changes what the new one has to be good at.

The Real Risk

The Traffic You Already Earned Is What You Can Lose

A redesign changes URLs, structure and copy at once. Done without care, the site loses rankings it took years to build, and the loss shows up a quarter later when nobody connects it to the launch.

  1. 01

    Inventory what currently earns

    Every URL with impressions, clicks, backlinks or conversions gets listed before anything is designed. Pages that earn nothing can be cut without ceremony. Pages that earn quietly are the ones a redesign usually deletes by accident.

  2. 02

    Map every old URL to a new one

    A one-to-one redirect map, written before launch rather than after the 404s appear. Redirecting everything to the home page is the usual shortcut and it throws away most of the equity it was meant to preserve.

  3. 03

    Keep the content that ranks

    If a page ranks, its substance moves across even when its design does not. Cutting a thousand words to fit a new template is how a site loses the position that was paying for itself.

  4. 04

    Watch the first ninety days

    Crawl weekly after launch, compare against the pre-launch baseline, and fix what moved. Most redesign damage is recoverable if it is caught in the first month and expensive once it is not.

This is also the argument for redesigning in stages where the site allows it: fewer variables changing at once, and a result you can still attribute afterwards.

Case Study

Six sites, run as one estate.

A move off K2 Group’s old domain had left rankings stranded behind it. 261 URLs were mapped to the brands that should own them, and the retired domain fell from 103 ranked terms to 3 as the group’s brand search moved to first place on the live site.
